title: Verifier-Guided Prompting for Intent-to-Configuration Translation: A Preregistered NetOps Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory trial (N=150 synthetic intents; shared_initial_candidate semantics) to test whether constrained prompting combined with deterministic verifier-guided iterative feedback (generate→verify→repair, one allowed repair) materially increases verifier-level semantic correctness for natural-language → low-level network-configuration translation. Model: gpt-5-mini; verifier: deterministic_netops_validator_v5; adapter family: hosted_netops_gvr_v1. For each intent a single initial model generation was shared across baseline and guarded conditions; the guarded pipeline could invoke at most one additional repair call if the verifier failed that initial candidate. Results (confirmatory): baseline = 149/150 (99.333%), guarded = 150/150 (100.0%); paired absolute difference = 0.0066667 (0.67 percentage points); exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap percentile CI = [0.00, 0.02] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Only one guarded repair invocation occurred (1/150); median revision iterations = 0 (IQR = 0). Interpretation: on this preregistered synthetic corpus the guarded workflow yielded a numerically negligible and statistically non-significant improvement over an already near-ceiling baseline. We bound this empirical outcome to the provided synthetic corpus, single model, shared_initial_candidate execution semantics, and deterministic validator and highlight the methodological lesson that pilot baseline calibration is necessary to avoid ceiling effects that invalidate preregistered power assumptions.

sections.introduction:
Natural-language intent interfaces aim to reduce NetOps friction by translating human operator intents into concrete low-level configuration sequences that can be executed or reviewed. Prior work documents that LLMs can produce useful configuration templates but often produce syntactic errors, omissions, or unsafe sequences that require downstream correction [1]. Deterministic verifier-guided generate→verify→repair pipelines are a common defensive architecture intended to detect and correct such errors prior to execution [2], [3]. Security analyses additionally motivate runtime gating because textual claims can map directly to tool calls in agentic LLM pipelines, creating claim-to-action vulnerabilities [4], [5].

Research question. Following a fresh literature synthesis we preregistered and executed the confirmatory question: Does constrained prompting (structured templates + semantic slots) combined with deterministic verifier-guided iterative feedback materially increase verifier-level semantic correctness of NL→configuration translation compared to an unconstrained baseline under a paired design? The design, analysis plan, and execution contract were frozen prior to observing outcomes (preregistration id: study_cand_2026_b2_v1; preregistration SHA-256 reported in the Disclosure Statement).

Contributions. (1) A fully preregistered paired confirmatory trial that measures deterministic-verifier pass/fail as the principal endpoint on an artifactized synthetic intent corpus. (2) A complete archived execution and preregistered analysis (N=150 paired items; completed episodes = 300; model calls used = 151) comparing baseline free-text prompting to constrained-template prompting plus at most one verifier-guided repair under shared_initial_candidate semantics. (3) An artifact-grounded empirical finding: on the supplied corpus the guarded pipeline produced a negligible numerical improvement (0.67 pp) over an already near-ceiling baseline; we emphasize the methodological implication that baseline competence must be piloted and calibrated to preserve statistical power in preregistered NetOps trials.
sections.related_work:
Our study intersects three strands of recent work. First, intent-to-configuration research documents the difficulty of converting free-text operator intents into verifier-sound artifacts and reports modest semantic-correctness rates on public benchmarks [1]. Second, generator-plus-verifier and iterative repair architectures for infrastructure-as-code and configuration repair show improved correctness when deterministic or policy-guided verifiers are integrated with model outputs [2], [6]. Third, security analyses of agentic LLM pipelines reveal claim-to-action and prompt-injection vulnerabilities that motivate runtime gating and auditable decision points [4], [5].

We position our trial to operationalize and preregister a tightly constrained generate→verify→repair intervention, using an explicit paired design and a deterministic validator as the confirmatory oracle so that numerical outcomes map directly to verifier-level semantic correctness. Compared with prior studies that report larger guarded-vs-baseline gains, our run differs in (a) the shared_initial_candidate execution semantics, (b) a one-repair budget per task, (c) a single tested model (gpt-5-mini), and (d) a synthetic verifier-capable task bank restricted to small topologies. These differences explain why our numerical bound on marginal repair benefit should be interpreted alongside, not as a contradiction to, prior work that used different sampling or repair budgets [2], [3].
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and design. The trial was preregistered as study_cand_2026_b2_v1 and frozen prior to observing model outputs (preregistration SHA-256 = aea996afce45e3798345f6e32ae6c347456f103ecdb84fc36e27bb486a329399). The confirmatory estimand is the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (guarded = constrained prompt + at most one verifier-guided repair; baseline = free-text prompt). Primary test: exact two-sided McNemar; 95% bootstrap percentile CI computed with 10,000 resamples (bootstrap_seed = 1729). Secondary contrasts were preregistered but not executed as confirmatory (constrained-only condition B was conceptually preregistered but not used for confirmatory inference in this run).

Shared_initial_candidate semantics and baseline interpretation. The execution contract used the shared_initial_candidate semantics: for each intent exactly one initial model generation was produced and that same sampled initial candidate was used to evaluate both baseline and guarded conditions. The guarded pipeline could invoke at most one additional repair call only if the deterministic verifier failed that initial candidate. Consequently, the observed baseline success rate measures the validity of that single initial sampled candidate; the guarded vs baseline contrast therefore isolates the marginal effect of the single allowed repair applied to the identical initial sample. This semantics (and its accounting) is recorded in deterministic_reconciliation.json and discussed explicitly in the archived artifacts.

Task bank and sampling. Confirmatory tasks: N=150 distinct synthetic intents generated deterministically by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5. Tasks cover four intent families (reachability/isolation, ACL-like changes, VLAN/MTU sequence changes, and uplink switchover patterns) and are restricted to verifier-capable small topologies (4–32 nodes). Inclusion/exclusion: a rule-based ambiguity detector and parser/verifier-coverage checks were applied deterministically prior to model calling; no confirmatory exclusions occurred in this run (exclusions = 0).

Model, validator, and runtime sampling semantics. Declared model: gpt-5-mini (provider record: openai_responses). Deterministic validator: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (validator_version = 5.0) used a full-intent-constraint validation rule that returns a boolean pass/fail and normalized configuration text. Important runtime-reporting clarification (reviewer-requested): the archived execution/model_configuration.json explicitly records declared_model_version = "gpt-5-mini" and temperature = null (unset). The run did not enforce a deterministic sampling temperature or fixed random-seed for the LLM; therefore model outputs may be nondeterministic across independent API sessions. All per-call runtime sampling metadata and provider-call logs are archived and identify model_call counts and per-call attributes.

Execution adapter and repair budget. The adapter_family = hosted_netops_gvr_v1 enforced an execution budget of exactly one initial model call per intent and at most one repair call per intent (planned episodes = 300; maximum_model_calls = 300). The run completed all planned episodes (completed_episode_count = 300) and observed a single repair-stage invocation (repair = 1). Each model call executed in an isolated API session and per-call metadata were recorded in execution/provider_calls and execution/responses artifacts.

Scoring and analysis plan. The deterministic validator produced normalized final configurations and a score_reason_code field; the primary outcome is verifier-level semantic correctness (binary pass/fail). Primary analysis used an exact McNemar two-sided test on the paired contingency table with 10,000 bootstrap resamples (seed = 1729) to generate a 95% percentile CI. The preregistered missingness plan used complete-pair analysis; no missing pairs occurred. All analysis code, paired_contingency_table.csv, and condition_summary.csv are archived in the analysis artifacts.
sections.results:
Execution accounting. Planned paired episodes = 300; completed_episode_count = 300; complete_pair_count = 150; model_calls_used = 151; repair-stage invocations observed = 1. No episodes failed or were excluded; analysis/missingness_summary.csv reports zero missing or unscorable episodes.

Primary numerical outcomes. Paired contingency counts (guarded × baseline): n_11 = 149 (both-pass), n_10 = 1 (guarded-only-pass), n_01 = 0 (baseline-only-pass), n_00 = 0 (both-fail). Per-condition success rates: baseline_success_count = 149/150 = 0.9933333333333333; guarded_success_count = 150/150 = 1.0. Estimated paired absolute difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.00666666666666671 (≈0.67 percentage points). Exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.0. Paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.00, 0.02] (10,000 resamples; bootstrap_seed = 1729). The analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv and analysis/condition_summary.csv files substantiate these counts.

Repair and revision diagnostics. Only one guarded repair invocation occurred (1/150), consistent with the near-ceiling initial success rate; median revision iterations in guarded episodes = 0 (IQR = 0). The single repair improved one initially invalid candidate to valid under the deterministic validator. Deterministic_reconciliation.json records provider-call auditing: hosted_model_call_event_count = 151; stage_counts: shared_initial_generation = 150, repair = 1; condition_counts: shared = 150, guarded = 1; all deterministic consistency checks passed.

Representative artifact-grounded examples. Representative tasks stored in the execution bundle illustrate typical intents and validator traces (e.g., task-000001, task-000002, task-000003). For task-000001 the intent was: "Migrate edge1 to VLAN 30 and MTU 1600. For safety, shut edge1 down before changing either VLAN or MTU, then restore it to admin up." The shared-initial and both condition responses produced the expected four-command sequence; validator_trace.validation_after recorded normalized_configuration matching the reference answer, parsed_command_count = 4, required_command_count = 4, and valid = true. Representative artifacts and SHA-256s are preserved in the execution manifest.

Execution audit summary (artifact-grounded). Execution audit metrics from deterministic_reconciliation and analysis artifacts: completed episodes = 300; complete pairs = 150; model calls used = 151; repair-stage invocations = 1; exclusions = 0; contamination flags = 0 (analysis/contamination_summary.csv empty). These counts confirm that the run adhered to the preregistered execution contract and the adapter's per-task call limits.
sections.discussion:
Ceiling effect and preregistration mismatch. The preregistered power analysis targeted detecting an absolute improvement of ≈15 percentage points with N=150 under an assumed baseline substantially below ceiling. Observed baseline initial-candidate success was 149/150 (≈99.33%), leaving minimal room for improvement and producing a ceiling effect that rendered the planned confirmatory contrast uninformative. This demonstrates the practical necessity of a small pilot baseline-calibration step in preregistered NetOps trials to align task difficulty and sample size with observed base-model competence.

Interpretation under shared_initial_candidate semantics. Under shared_initial_candidate semantics both conditions evaluated the identical initial sampled candidate for each intent; the guarded pipeline could improve outcomes only by applying the single allowed repair when the verifier failed that initial candidate. Therefore the marginal effect we estimate is strictly the additional benefit obtainable from at most one repair applied to the same initial generation. Alternative semantics (independent per-condition sampling, larger repair budgets, or multiple iterative repair rounds) could allow greater observable differences and remain important directions for future confirmatory designs.

Operational implications beyond pass/fail rates. Even when guarded pipelines yield marginal numerical improvements under verifier pass/fail metrics, they still provide operational benefits that are not captured by the single binary endpoint: auditable decision records, enforced gating points for human approval, standardized verifier verdicts for downstream automation, and explicit repair prompts that can feed into operator dashboards. These non-statistical benefits can be operationally valuable even when a numerical difference is near-zero on a synthetic corpus.

Relation to prior empirical work. Our artifact-grounded outcome does not conflict with prior reports of larger gains from verifier-guided repair [2], [6]; those studies typically evaluate settings with lower baseline generation competence, different sampling semantics, richer repair channels, or multi-iteration feedback. Our contribution is a narrowly bounded empirical measurement of a single-repair guarded pipeline under shared_initial_candidate semantics with gpt-5-mini on a deterministic synthetic corpus and deterministic validator.

Threats to validity (expanded). Internal: shared_initial_candidate semantics were chosen to isolate marginal repair effect but do not measure inter-condition sampling variance. Construct: verifier pass/fail is a machine-checkable proxy for semantic correctness but depends on mapping code and the validator's coverage; mapping or validator bugs would bias measurements (the execution bundle includes unit-tests and mapping code checks run pre-execution). External: single-model (gpt-5-mini), synthetic tasks, and small topologies (4–32 nodes) limit claims about production WANs and vendor-specific CLIs. Conclusion validity: preregistered power assumptions were invalidated by the ceiling baseline; the exact McNemar p = 1.0 and bootstrap CI = [0.00, 0.02] quantify the limited inferential power for larger effects in this setting.

Practical guidance for future preregistered NetOps trials. Based on these artifact-grounded findings we recommend (1) a short pilot phase to estimate baseline initial-candidate correctness with the chosen model and prompts prior to locking sample size; (2) clearly specified generation semantics (shared_initial_candidate vs independent sampling) aligned with the estimand of interest; (3) explicit repair-budget sensitivity analyses (one vs multiple repairs) in the preregistration; and (4) validator-coverage tests and mapping unit-tests run and archived prior to model calls to avoid contamination by transformer/translation errors.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered paired confirmatory trial comparing baseline free-text prompting to constrained-template prompting plus a single verifier-guided repair under shared_initial_candidate semantics. On the archived synthetic corpus with gpt-5-mini and a deterministic validator, the guarded pipeline increased verifier pass rate from 149/150 to 150/150 (0.67 percentage points), a numerically tiny and statistically non-significant difference (exact McNemar p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap CI = [0.00, 0.02]). The principal scientific lesson is methodological: preregistered LLM-for-NetOps trials should include pilot baseline calibration so that task difficulty and sample size preserve statistical power and avoid ceiling effects. Technically, our artifacts bound the marginal benefit of a single-repair guarded pipeline under shared_initial_candidate semantics; evaluating independent-sampling semantics, larger repair budgets, model diversity, and production-scale topologies remains important future work.

limitations: Single-model constraint: experiments used only gpt-5-mini; results do not generalize across models or sizes.

Synthetic corpus and scale: tasks were programmatically generated and limited to verifier-capable toy-to-small topologies (4–32 nodes); external validity to production WANs and heterogeneous vendor CLIs is untested.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics and execution contract limited repair budget to at most one guarded repair call per intent; different generation semantics or multiple-repair budgets may yield different outcomes.

Ceiling effect and preregistration mismatch: baseline correctness was far higher than the pilot assumptions used for power calculations (planned detectable effect = 15 percentage points), reducing the trial's ability to demonstrate benefit and illustrating sensitivity to baseline calibration.

Verifier coverage and specification translation: the study measures deterministic validator pass/fail on the preregistered invariants but does not claim safety guarantees beyond the deterministic validator's modeled properties.

Security and adversarial robustness: the experiment did not evaluate adversarial prompt-injection or adversary-driven intents; separate targeted studies are required to assess claim-to-action vulnerabilities in agentic NetOps workflows.
